cultivar: Clonal and Chinary bushes (AV2, B157, T78)
processing: Partly oxidised to no fixed level, with long withers, some bruising, gentle rolling and a light drying; a few makers ball-roll in the Taiwanese manner or add a light roast.
harvest_season: Spring and autumn lots are best; some summer production.
appearance_dry: Loosely twisted or semi-rolled leaf, olive-brown with silver tips.
taste_profile: Fruity and floral with honey, apricot and a creamy softness; very low in bitterness.

brewing.notes: Also excellent gongfu style (6 g per 120 ml, short steeps), where it gives five or six infusions.

vintage_note: Sold by factory, season and year as small lots, usually at a premium over the black teas from the same place (Jun Chiyabari's oolongs are the ones most often named); drink within a year or two. There is no standard oxidation level, so compare descriptions before buying.
description:
Nepal oolong is what the more adventurous factories of Ilam and Dhankuta make when they take their Darjeeling-style spring processing and push it deliberately towards the Chinese and Taiwanese model: longer withers, some bruising, controlled partial oxidation and a gentle finish. The results range from almost-white to almost-black, and the better ones are among the most interesting teas Nepal makes.

Oxidation has no fixed level; some makers ball-roll the leaf Taiwanese style, a few add a light roast, most leave it twisted and unroasted. The leaf comes from the same clonal and Chinary bushes as the black teas, and the spring and autumn lots are the best.

The cup is golden amber, fruity and floral: apricot, honey, white flowers and a creamy softness with very little bitterness. Brew it Western style at about 90 °C for three minutes, or gongfu style with short steeps, where it will give five or six infusions.

It is sold by factory, season and year as small lots, usually at a premium over the black teas from the same place; Jun Chiyabari's oolongs are the ones most often named. Drink within a year or two. As with Darjeeling oolong, there is no standard, so compare descriptions before you buy.

A natural next step for Darjeeling first-flush drinkers who want more sweetness and less grip.
history:
Oolong is a recent experiment in Nepal, with no long local tradition behind it, and when it began is not well documented. The name most tied to it is Jun Chiyabari, a garden in Dhankuta founded in 2000, which planted cultivars from Taiwan and Japan as well as local ones.

Other Nepalese oolongs reach Western lists under seller names such as Moon Drops and Jade Oolong. The category has no fixed standard, so the word covers quite different teas.
